report:
## Conclusion

The claim that having an abortion increases a woman's risk of breast cancer is **not supported by the current scientific consensus**. Major medical organizations and the weight of high-quality evidence indicate no causal link between induced abortion and breast cancer.

## Evidence

The American Cancer Society states that "the most up-to-date scientific research suggests that abortion does not influence a woman's risk for breast cancer," noting that a 2018 report from the U.S. National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine reached the same conclusion and that "higher-quality studies have generally found no link" (https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html).

Susan G. Komen for the Cure reports that findings from cohort studies, a meta-analysis, and a large pooled analysis show no increased breast cancer risk associated with abortion or miscarriage (https://www.komen.org/breast-cancer/facts-statistics/research-studies/topics/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk/).

Breastcancer.org similarly states plainly that "evidence shows that there's no link between having an abortion and developing breast cancer" (https://www.breastcancer.org/risk/risk-factors/abortion).

The National Cancer Institute's position, as summarized by Wikipedia, is that the abortion–breast cancer hypothesis "is at odds with mainstream scientific opinion and is rejected by major medical professional organizations" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion–breast_cancer_hypothesis).

Some older case-control studies and a few meta-analyses (e.g., Brind et al.) reported a positive association, but these have been criticized for reporting bias. Prospective studies and nationwide registry data, including a recent Finnish population-based study, have not confirmed any increased risk.
